description.purpose: What is on the screen right now, as one table of rows. Eight slots per view: `owner` (the `envelope.reply_to` of whoever put it up -- never a field out of a body), `view_id` (that sender's own name for it, `[a-z0-9-]{1,64}`), `region` (where on the screen; v1 knows one, `main`), `kind` (`prose` or `component`), `content` (the prose `{title, body}`, or the root node of a component tree), `components` (the `component.define` arguments the view brought with it, so a later write can be compared against them and skipped when nothing changed), `ttl_ms` (how long the view stays fresh; `0` is forever) and `updated_at` (epoch milliseconds, which is what orders the screen newest first).
description.use_when: Inside a display hive only. The compose cell is the sole reader and the sole writer; a second writer would be a second opinion about what is on the screen, and the screen has only one.
description.not_in_scope: It decides nothing and enforces nothing. IDENTITY IS `(owner, view_id)`, and this cell cannot say so: a store schema declaration carries column types and nothing else -- no PRIMARY KEY, no UNIQUE, no index -- so the uniqueness is held by `compose`, which writes a view as a DELETE on that pair followed by an INSERT, in one bundle, in that order. A bundle is not a transaction, which is why the select that reads the before-state is the FIRST leg rather than a second round trip. Nothing here sweeps either: an expired row stays until something overwrites it, and it simply stops being drawn.
